source.title: Synergy and Symmetry in Deep Learning: Interactions between the Data, Model, and Inference Algorithm

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies width sweeps and architecture comparisons to CIFAR-10 and ImageNet settings not specified in the claim versions, and reports how test performance changes.
record.gate_note: Own experiments compare architectures and report width-dependent test accuracy. The paper does not test random-label memorization, optimizer comparisons among adaptive methods, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Some numerical results appear only in figures; cited results from prior work were not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares convolutional and fully connected networks trained with momentum SGD on CIFAR-10, bearing on V3. Its convolutional width sweeps measure a related trend, but do not establish V2's prerequisite of widening beyond zero training error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that learning efficiency depends on consistency among data, model, and inference algorithm. Their width experiments show symmetry-dependent benefits or penalties from widening; their broader conclusion also emphasizes that additional data can improve learning-curve slopes, suggesting transitions toward more data-efficient learned function classes.
record.recipe_differences: Eight-hidden-layer architectures and CIFAR-10 experiments; the paper studies symmetry and data/model/inference interactions rather than the specified random-label generalization setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Width effects differ between untransformed and O(3)d-transformed data. In CIFAR-10 experiments, larger learning rate and L2 regularization affect performance and small-width variability. The authors report that the particular sampled rotation has negligible effect across runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing from infinite-width NTK regression to finite-width NN+ raises GAP accuracy from 77% to 84% and VEC accuracy from 67% to 78%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finite-width convolutional networks trained with a larger learning rate and L2 regularization can outperform their infinite-width NTK counterparts on unaugmented CIFAR-10.

record.problems: Width-sweep accuracy values are presented in figures without text-stated exact values. CIFAR-10 width-sweep runs were selected among successful runs with training accuracy ≥95%, rather than uniformly reporting all runs; some configurations had only one or two successful runs. The study does not locate a zero-training-error interpolation threshold for the width sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Other reported CIFAR-10 architecture and data-transformation comparisons are largely figure-only, and the text does not state model-specific accuracy values that can be assigned reliably to individual architectures and conditions under the row limit.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the paired comparison with natural-label held-out performance.
The post-zero-training-error width trend in converged, unregularized one-hidden-layer networks. The convolutional sweeps do not establish the interpolation threshold.
Whether local connectivity accounts for most of the convolutional advantage; fully connected networks learning sparse local connections; initialization from trained convolutional networks.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover large-batch performance.
Dropout effects, small-data exceptions, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus matched random removals.

missing.what: Direct finite-width GAP-versus-FCN accuracy comparisons under NN and NN+, with architecture widths and training conditions. Architecture comparisons are acknowledged in rows_left_out, but rows are needed to represent the V3 result supporting the verdict.
missing.locator: Section 3.1; Sections 5.1–5.3 and Figure 2; Supplement B.1

record.verdict_notes: No V2 support or challenge verdict is warranted without establishing its zero-training-error prerequisite. R5–R6 cannot justify a V3 limits_scope verdict because they compare inference procedures within convolutional architectures. Exact Figure 2 and Figure 3 coordinates cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test performance.
Tests eight-hidden-layer convolutional VEC networks on CIFAR-10, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10; does not identify the width needed for zero training error.
Does not test learned sparse local connections or initialize a fully connected network from a trained convolutional network.
No adaptive optimizer comparison or broad optimizer tuning.
No large-batch comparison or fixed-epoch batch-size experiment.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization measures.

rows.note: The text says performance decreases monotonically and dramatically after a width threshold toward or across NTK performance. Exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Accuracy decreases beyond approximately width 64, but the study does not establish zero training error across these widths. Thus the reported reversal in the width trend cannot establish reversal of V2's post-interpolation effect. Reported accuracies select the best test checkpoint among runs reaching at least 95% training accuracy.

rows.subject: GAP∞
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy across architectures and inference algorithms on CIFAR-10.
rows.note: The paper reports 77% → 84% for GAP∞ → GAPn when changing from NTK to NN+. This is an inference-algorithm comparison within an architecture, not a direct FCN-versus-convolution comparison.
rows.check: This compares infinite-width GAP under NTK regression, 77%, with finite-width GAP under NN+, 84%; it does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks. The subject should identify finite-width GAP as the model producing the recorded value.

relationships.condition: Eight-hidden-layer networks trained from scratch with momentum SGD on untransformed CIFAR-10.
relationships.reason: Based on the text rather than R5–R6: Section 3.1 explicitly reports that this study also finds GAP outperforming FCN, LCN, and VEC in Section 5; the direct architecture comparisons require rows.
relationships.display_finding: The reported advantage of the model using global average pooling (GAP) over fully connected (FCN) models, locally connected (LCN) models and models with vectorized outputs (VEC) remains unverified.
